_note: SAMPLE. Generated from the hypothesised draft so the pages can be built and reviewed before Thursday. Replaced by live data on draft day.

roast.text: Keshia took the best quarterback alive with the third pick in the draft, which is the correct move and therefore deeply suspicious. Six straight years of Allen finishing first or second, and she found him anyway. We're logging this as a lucky mouse click and moving on.

Jay took Jonathan Taylor, a guy who led the league in carries and touchdowns, and did it at the exact spot where everyone in the room expected him to go. No hesitation, no risk, no fingerprints. He drafted like a man reading the instructions out loud.

Justin took the only guy in history with 90 catches in each of his first five seasons, which required him to do nothing but not look away. He's finished third among receivers three years running. Justin picked the name at the top and we're treating that as a clerical accident rather than a plan.

Mike wanted Jalen Hurts and nobody was going to stop him, so he stopped himself. Hurts ran for 421 yards last year after four straight seasons of 600-plus, and his fantasy scoring hit its lowest point as a starter. James Cook III sat right there watching Mike outbid an empty room.
Evan took the best player on the board. Suspiciously competent.

For Chris Olave to pay off here, the career year has to repeat, the health has to hold, and Breece Hall and Ashton Jeanty both have to quietly disappoint from someone else's bench. Bree needs three things to go right and walked past thirty guys who only needed one. That's not a plan, that's a wish with a receiver attached.

Jesse took Travis Etienne, a fine back who just moved to New Orleans, and paid a price that suggested nobody else was allowed to want him. Ashton Jeanty was sitting there the whole time. Jesse looked at a better player and a longer relationship with his own team and chose neither.

Chenell drafted Nico Collins on the theory that Jayden Higgins's torn ACL makes him the whole Houston passing game, which is a lot of faith in a guy who's never played all seventeen. She stepped over CeeDee Lamb to get there. Defending champ, building around somebody else's injury report.

Evan followed up the safest running back on the board with the most famous quarterback on it. Mahomes averaged 15 points a game over his last six and tore his ACL in Week 15, and he's still the name your uncle would say first. Evan isn't drafting a roster, he's drafting the guys on the pregame graphic.

That's four quarterbacks for Mike, in a league that starts two on a good day. He's now got a bench that could run a full scrimmage and nobody to hand off to. Somewhere in there is a plan to trade one of these guys to a man who already has three.

Colin took the Offensive Rookie of the Year, which sounds great until you notice the guy finished 16th among receivers and managed exactly one top-10 week all season. For this to work, Carolina has to become a real offense, the leap everybody's promising has to actually happen, and Justin Herbert has to be no use to anyone. Colin's betting on a player whose best trait so far is that people keep saying his name.

Keshia grabbed Jared Goff, a guy with three straight 4,500-yard seasons, at a spot where nobody left on the board was better. That's twice now. Two correct picks is no longer a lucky mouse click, it's a pattern, and we're deeply uncomfortable about it.

Tyler wanted DJ Moore badly enough to reach past Garrett Wilson for a guy whose target share last year was the smallest since he was a rookie. Moore's in Buffalo now, behind Khalil Shakir, hoping the change of scenery does the work. Tyler paid a premium for a receiver whose whole case is that things can only get better.

Justin took Harold Fannin Jr., which puts him one Njoku away from just owning the Cleveland tight end room outright. Fannin was terrific as a 21-year-old rookie and Justin skipped George Pickens to lock him in early. Last pick was the safest name on the board, this one's a sophomore tight end. He's not building a roster, he's collecting whichever guy he read about most recently.

For Tony Pollard to work here, Tennessee's offense has to wake up, the touchdowns have to triple, and Tyjae Spears has to stop existing. Colin needs all three, and he skipped Zay Flowers and George Kittle, who each needed nothing. He's also got one quarterback in a league that starts two, so the copium's getting passed around the whole roster.

Somewhere in Seattle, Sam Darnold finished fifth in the league in passing yards and 27th among quarterbacks in fantasy points per game, and Bree looked at that gap and saw an opportunity. She's still got one starter for two quarterback slots, so this is the fix. Last time she needed three things to go right. Now she needs Darnold to have nine fewer bad weeks than he had.

Doug now has five running backs, one quarterback, and one receiver, which is a fantasy team the way a bag of flour is a cake. Tuten's the best guy on the board, sure, and he cleared ten touches once in fifteen games last year. Every Sunday Doug gets to start two backs and leave three of them home wondering.

Chenell took DK Metcalf, who missed two games and posted a career-low 850 yards, and walked past Sam LaPorta to do it. The defending champ has three backs, three receivers, a tight end and not one quarterback in a format that starts two. She's assembling a beautiful skill-position collection and nobody to throw to any of it.

Jameson Williams is a genuinely good pick, and he's also Tyler's fifth receiver. Two receiver slots, one flex, five guys. Tyler's built a wideout depth chart and forgot to attach a football team to the bottom of it.

James drafted Luther Burden III on the strength of a rookie year where he barely played, which is the fantasy equivalent of falling in love with a highlight reel. Two career top-20 games. Burden also picked up a groin injury on a contested red-zone rep in August. James walked past Rome Odunze to buy a guy on the promise of what he flashed.

Mike finally drafted a receiver, his fifth quarterback ago. For Tee Higgins to pay off, Cincinnati has to keep throwing at a guy who's missed seven games in two years, Ja'Marr Chase has to leave a few scraps near the goal line, and Mike has to find somebody willing to take a quarterback off his hands. That's five arms, one back, one wideout, and a trade offer nobody in this league is answering.

Evan took Rhamondre Stevenson, a guy who started thirteen games and still got out-touched by the rookie behind him, which is the least famous thing Evan has done all draft. He's got one quarterback for two quarterback slots and keeps buying running backs like the second slot will fill itself. The pregame graphic isn't going to hand him another Mahomes.

James took the other half of the New England backfield, a guy who was great in three games and a spectator in fourteen. Henderson did lead that committee on touch share, 25.1% to Stevenson's 18.9%, so James has bought the better slice of a pie nobody's finished baking. Second straight pick built on flashes, and he still hasn't gotten around to a second quarterback.

Colin took Mark Andrews, a tight end who played all seventeen games and remains genuinely good, which after Pollard and the copium roster reads like somebody else logged into his account. Nothing had to go right for this one. He's now got two tight ends for one tight end slot and one quarterback for two, so the competence was clearly a slip.
Round 8 and Bree still has 1 quarterback in a superflex league. Bold.

Chenell took Jaylen Warren, who splits the Pittsburgh backfield with Rico Dowdle, a man Bree drafted one pick earlier. So she's now got half of a committee and zero quarterbacks in a league that starts two. The defending champ has four running backs, three receivers, a tight end, and nobody under center to hand any of it the ball.

Kyle Monangai had one enormous game and Bree drafted the guy from that Sunday, not the one averaging 6.9 touches the rest of the year. She's still stacking tight ends she can't start and running backs behind other running backs. First it was three things going right, then it was Darnold's nine bad weeks, now she needs D'Andre Swift to vanish.

Marvin Harrison Jr. has finished 41st and 39th among receivers in his two seasons, and Jay looked at that and saw a fourth overall pick worth owning. He walked past Isaiah Likely to do it. The man who drafted Jonathan Taylor by reading the instructions out loud has discovered the draft-day scratch ticket, and picked the one everybody already scratched.

James took Michael Wilson on the basis of eight games with Jacoby Brissett throwing to him while Marvin Harrison was hurt, and Harrison went three picks ago to somebody else. That's three straight picks on guys who flashed once. He's got one quarterback for two starting slots and twenty-six better players sitting there, but the flash reel needed another chapter.

Xavier Worthy got hurt on his third snap last year and reached twelve fantasy points once in fourteen games, and Jay walked past Josh Jacobs for the privilege. That's five receivers for two slots and a flex, next to one quarterback in a format that starts two. The guy who used to read the instructions has thrown the manual out and is now just buying Kansas City merchandise.

Aaron Jones was the best player left, and Bree took him, which after the wish list and the Darnold math reads like she hit the wrong button on the way to something worse. He was dead last among sixty-five backs in forced missed tackle rate, so even the correct pick came with a hedge attached. Three tight ends, one quarterback, and one accidental piece of competence.

Chenell drafted Michael Pittman, who's now in Pittsburgh, where she already owns half that backfield. She stepped over Josh Jacobs to add another Steeler to a team that still has nobody to throw or hand it to. The defending champ is building a very tasteful Pittsburgh gift shop with one quarterback in the back room.

Doug took Stefon Diggs, a receiver, which for him counts as branching out. Josh Jacobs was sitting right there and Doug already had five running backs, so the one time the stud fell to him he finally didn't want one. The bag of flour now has a receiver in it. Still not a cake.

Jesse took Josh Jacobs, the best guy on the board, and stapled him onto a pile that already had four backs and three quarterbacks. That's five running backs for two slots and a flex, plus a third quarterback to watch them not play. Every position he's overloaded, he's overloaded twice.

Doug followed Diggs with Rachaad White, who plays for the same Washington team, so he's now hedging his receiver with a running back and hedging that running back with the six he already owns. That's seven backs for two slots and a flex. He isn't drafting a roster, he's buying up an entire NFL depth chart one confused position at a time.

Kenny Gainwell was the best player available and Chenell took him, which makes five running backs and still not one additional quarterback. She's had eleven rounds to notice the format starts two. The defending champ has built the deepest handoff-receiving corps in the league and nobody legally able to hand off.

Bree took Croskey-Merritt with nobody better on the board, which is twice in one stretch that she's done the sensible thing. Nothing has to go right here. No missed weeks, no vanishing teammate, no nine-game reversal from a quarterback in Seattle. The streak of wishes ends quietly, and she's still got one quarterback and three tight ends to remember it by.

Evan Engram finished fifteenth or worse among tight ends in routes, targets, catches and yards, and Jay wanted him badly enough to do it forty-four picks before anyone in Denver would have. He walked past Blake Corum for a guy who scored once near the goal line all year. First he read the instructions out loud, then he threw the manual out, and now he's writing his own in crayon.

MarShawn Lloyd has played one game since 2024 and James bought him ten picks after Jesse bought Josh Jacobs, so he's paying full price for the backup on somebody else's team. Aaron Rodgers was there, a quarterback, for the man with one quarterback and two slots. Four picks now built on things that almost happened.

Justin took Brian Thomas Jr., who was fantasy's fourth-best receiver with Mac Jones throwing and a middling flex guy with Trevor Lawrence, and Justin already owns half the receiver room in the league. That's five receivers for two slots, two tight ends for one. The guy who kept picking whichever name he read about most recently has now read about everybody.

Jordan Addison's targets, catches, yards and touchdowns have all gone down two years running, so naturally James saw a guy who flashed once as a rookie and had to have him. That's six receivers for two slots and a flex, sitting next to one quarterback in a format that starts two. The flash reel is now a boxed set nobody can play on Sunday.

Jerry Jeudy has finished outside the top 50 receivers four times in six years and dropped 32 passes doing it, and Colin decided round twelve was the moment to plant his flag. Khalil Shakir was there. Cam Ward was there, a quarterback, in a league that starts two. Andrews was the slip, this is Colin back to his actual religion.

Wan'Dale Robinson is a slot guy who catches ninety balls a year and never sees the goal line, which is a fine thing to own and a strange thing to keep buying. Tyler walked past Quentin Johnston to make it six receivers for two slots and a flex, and he's got one running back in the whole building. The wideout depth chart is now three pages long and the backfield is a Post-it.

Calvin Ridley missed ten games and caught seventeen passes, a career low, and Jay looked at that wreckage and thought: sixth receiver. Cam Ward was sitting right there, a quarterback, for the man who still has one of those and two slots to fill. The crayon manual now has a chapter on why quarterbacks are optional.

Keshia paired Khalil Shakir with the Josh Allen she took third overall, which is the first thing all draft she's done that looks like a plan instead of an accident. Nobody better was on the board, again. Three correct picks and a stack, and the rest of the room is starting to suspect she's been reading something.

Jalen Nailor has never cleared 30 catches in a season and now gets to fight Tre Tucker, Jack Bech and Dont'e Thornton for snaps in Las Vegas, and Doug bought him twenty-nine better players early. Gunnar Helm was there, a tight end, for a man who owns zero tight ends and seven running backs. The bag of flour has gone out and bought a fourth-string Raider.

Oronde Gadsden had two enormous weeks in October and averaged 6.2 points the rest of the way, which is exactly the kind of thing James can't say no to. Chris Godwin was sitting right there. Five straight picks now built on a good month, and the man still has one quarterback for two starting slots, because the quarterbacks all had the bad manners to be consistent.

Deebo Samuel is back in San Francisco after a year of being solid and forgettable, and he's the fifth receiver Evan has stacked up for two slots and a flex. Three tight ends for one tight end spot on top of it. He isn't building a lineup, he's building a group photo of guys you'd recognize.

Evan took the Broncos defense in the fourteenth round, which is fine, except he took it 790 players early and it's the second Denver-adjacent name he's grabbed off a screen. RJ Harvey was there. The pregame graphic has stopped listing players and started listing entire units.

James used a pick on the Seahawks defense, eleven guys who aren't allowed to throw a forward pass, while his lineup still has one quarterback and two slots that want one. RJ Harvey was there, so was Romeo Doubs, so was the whole rest of the league. He's spent fourteen rounds collecting almosts and finished by drafting a group of men whose entire job is stopping somebody else's quarterback.

Colin took the Rams defense, which is fine, except he's now got four tight ends and one place to put them, and he skipped RJ Harvey to make it worse. The religion has a new commandment: never own a player who could plausibly start. Andrews was the slip, Jeudy was the relapse, and this is Colin building a chapel out of guys he can't field.

Jay drafted eleven guys from Detroit whose job is to stop a quarterback, which is the closest he's come all draft to acknowledging quarterbacks exist. He's still got one for two slots, six receivers for three spots, and a Sunday where somebody has to sit in the OP chair and pretend. The crayon manual now says the second quarterback slot can be filled with vibes.

Bree took the Eagles defense with RJ Harvey sitting there, which is a small crime next to what's happening on her own roster. Four tight ends. One tight end slot. One quarterback and two places that want one. The wishes came back, and this time she needs the league to change its lineup rules.

Jesse took the Chargers defense, eleven more men from Los Angeles to sit near his six running backs. He walked past RJ Harvey, an actual back, which would have been a seventh, so credit for restraint in the one place he has none. He's not building a roster anymore, he's building a regional fan club with a bench.

For Brandon Aubrey to be worth this, Dallas has to stall inside the thirty every week, the kicker has to out-score half of Jesse's backfield, and Jesse has to not notice he owns six running backs who all want the same two slots. He needs all three. He got the kicker eighty-five picks before anyone in Dallas would have bothered. The regional fan club now has a guy who kicks it.

Doug took a kicker with a questionable tag on him, which is a new kind of ambition. RJ Harvey was there, a running back, and Doug owns seven of those already, so passing on him might be the only disciplined thing he's done all night. The bag of flour has hired a guy to kick it.

For Jason Myers to matter, Seattle has to drive and then refuse to score, the defending champ's two tight ends have to fight it out for one slot, and five running backs have to reduce to three. Chenell needs all of that, plus RJ Harvey to have been the wrong answer. The gift shop is fully stocked and now sells a man who kicks field goals for Seattle.

Bree filled her kicker slot before she filled her second quarterback slot, which tells you exactly where Ka'imi Fairbairn ranks in the plan. One quarterback, two slots that start one each, and four tight ends waiting to be told which of them isn't playing. She spent all draft needing three things to go right and finished by drafting a guy who only needs the offense to fail.

Jay walked past RJ Harvey for Eddy Pineiro, a kicker in San Francisco, a place where the ball tends to reach the end zone without him. That's six receivers, three tight ends, one quarterback and now a foot. The crayon manual is finished, and the last page just says: the kicker will sort it out.

James closed out fifteen rounds of almosts with Jake Bates, and still hasn't found a second quarterback for the second quarterback slot. RJ Harvey was there. So was the rest of the league. He's built a lineup where the guy who kicks it is more certain to play than the guy who throws it.
